What changed and why"; `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-leftovers/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why".

- F-356 **In the fork/join shape that the library and the compiled runtime give parallel work, a Java model of microGPT's step with unboxed arrays runs 19 to 80 times slower than plain loops at the library's grains, and 1.4 to 4.8 times slower with the matrix product stopped at blocks of 16.** The library's range stops its split at 16 elements (`grainSize`, `Library/RangeInternals.fss`; P-175), and its matrix product splits down to single elements (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3044-3102`). The model is the baseline of F-355 with its vocabulary on a `ForkJoinPool` and plain loops at the leaves, so its times are a floor for compiled Fortress with this structure. At the library's grains a step takes 19 to 32 times the plain step on one thread, 55 times on two and 80 on four. Threads gain only from a product of about 128 by 128 with blocks of 64, and a dot product only from about 260,000 elements with a grain of 1,024; the model's products are 16 by 16 to 64 by 16. So at microGPT's sizes the library's parallel shape costs time at any thread count, and the matrix product's missing grain is the largest part of the cost. Measured once on a shared machine of 4 CPUs; every configuration passes the checks. Commands: `java-baseline/run.sh steps`, `kernels` and `scale`. Detail: `java-baseline/REPORT.md`, "6. Fork/join: the baseline in the shape of the library and the compiled runtime".

- F-364 **The compiled checker instantiates a reduction that writes no static argument by its expected type, else by the type of its body, where the call as written is not accepted; a reduction that is accepted as written is unchanged.** For `__bigOperator(BIG OP(), clauses)` with no static argument written, `reductionApplication` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala`) first checks the call as written, where the big operator has an instance alone; if that is not accepted or its type does not convert to the expected type, it writes the static argument as the expected type, then as the body's type, each only where the type meets the bounds of the big operator's one static parameter, and takes the first form that is accepted and converts. - F-365 **The compiled checker instantiates a reference to a generic function by the arrow type that receives it, and refuses one that the arrow type leaves open.** A functional reference with one declaration that has static parameters, no written static arguments and an expected arrow type takes the static arguments that make its instance a subtype of that type (`instantiatedReference`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala`); as an argument it is typed again in the retry with each candidate's parameter type (`retypable`). A static parameter that the arrow type's domain does not fix, one that only the return type mentions among them, is refused: 'A reference to the generic function pick takes its static arguments from the arrow type that receives it, and ZZ32->ZZ32 does not fix B.' An arrow type that carries its own static parameters is a subtype of no arrow type and coerces to nothing (`scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala`, `scala_src/typechecker/CoercionOracle.scala:292-293`). The applied value of an untyped binding is refused with a message. A static parameter of the function's own counts as unbound also where the kind environment holds its name for another declaration's parameter, as inside a generic declaration that calls its static parameter the same (`carriesOwnStaticParams`, `TypeAnalyzer.scala`), and the memo of normalized arrow types keys an arrow type by its static parameters too, so that a generic function's type and an instance written alike are not taken for each other. +- F-366 **A numeral at a call goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, on both paths: a declaration that only the numeral's own coercion reaches runs in place of the one that fits the numeral at its default where its declared parameter types lie strictly below, by subtyping; otherwise the one that the default fits runs.** It builds P-46. So `u = 0` and `0 = u` are `true`, and `u =/= 0` is `false`, for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32`; `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`; `k(5)` runs `k(x: NN32)` beside `k(x: Any)`; a `case` clause `0` matches a zero `NN32`; and a program's own number type with a numeral coercion compares with a numeral by its own `=`. `Equality[\T\]` declares `opr =/=(self, other:T)` as the negation of the type's `=` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:102`), which a type that extends `Equality` reaches before the `=/=` over `Any` (`:98`). So a model line may compare a number of any type with a numeral, and write a float numeral beside an integer value, on both paths. The checker does the comparison only where the declaration that fits has a numeral at a parameter that is not of the numeral's default type, so a call such as `i + 1` costs nothing more; walk keeps each choice in its dispatch cache, except one that asked a type of a program's own for its numeral coercion, whose `where` clause the cache's key does not hold. The key tells a negative constant from a numeral of the same default, since no unsigned type takes the first (`Numerals.rangeKey`). Two departures: under walk a numeral beside a value typed `Any` is converted by the value's run-time type (row 1016), and on both paths a numeral at a bare type parameter's declaration does not go to a more specific one (row 1017). +- P-46 **A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits, except a numeral's own conversion.** The declaration that runs is chosen on the parameter types that each overload declares: first those that apply, then the most specific of them (P-45). A generic declaration applies if some type within its bounds takes the arguments. Only then is the chosen declaration instantiated by promotion: at the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce (P-74). So beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` applies to a call with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, at `T = Number`. It is the more specific, so it runs, at `ZZ64`. Why: the curator wants fast generic code that a JVM can specialise. The exception is a numeral at a call. A comparison of a number with a numeral answers by the number's value, and the programmer does not retype the numeral: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, and no way that answers `false` is accepted. Of the ways to `true` that the review of them offers, the curator took its way B, whose rule is in the review's words, not his: a numeral is applicable to a parameter that fixes no type, at its default, and to a parameter whose type declares a coercion from the numeral's type, by that coercion (P-173); among the applicable declarations the most specific runs, and where two are not ordered, the one that the default fits. So `NN32`'s own `=` runs, and not the library's `=` over `(Any, Any)`, which the numeral fits at its default `ZZ32` and which answers `false` by `SEQV` (P-168). A value typed `Any` or `Number` fixes no type for the numeral beside it, which keeps its default. His own broader rule, to apply any conversion that reaches a specific declaration and to fall back to a plain one only when none does, so holds for a numeral's own conversion; for a value's coercion it is not taken. Walk and the compiled checker both infer static arguments with coercion, by the same promotion. The compiled path inserts the conversions statically. P-49 gives the order in which the checker tries a call. Row 537: the compiled dispatch between two generic declarations of one name with different bounds. Rows 973 and 966: walk answers `false` for `u = 0`, and `true` for `u =/= 0`, which follows `=`. Detail: `reviews/numeral-equality-ways-2026-11-10.md`, "Way B. A numeral goes to the most specific declaration that takes it; the default is the last resort".
+- P-78 **`SUM` and `PROD` are one generic reduction each over the library's algebra, in place of the team's catch-all over `Number`, and take their identity from the static argument.** `SUM` is generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `PROD` over `MultiplicativeRing`. A reduction written with generators writes its static argument where nothing at the call fixes the element type. The compiled checker fixes it from neither the generators, the body nor a declared type that receives the value, and refuses every such `SUM` or `PROD` that leaves it out (row 731, a gap of the checker). Row 731's workaround is to write it in every clause form of `SUM` and `PROD`, as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. A sum without generators is written as before, with no static argument: `SUM e` over a collection `e`, and the dot product `x DOT y`. `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN`, the team's `Number`-typed big operators for the maximum, the minimum and both, each with an identity, are gone; no program called them. `MAX` and `MIN` get no identity on the integers or the floats, so an empty `BIG MAX` or `BIG MIN` raises `EmptyReduction` (F-60: a maximum's identity is its type's least value, which a coercion into a wider type does not carry). Under walk, an empty `SUM` or `PROD` over another algebra, such as a user `AdditiveGroup`, still fails (row 436) until the specification's `HasIdentity` is built.
+- P-79 **Every team demo is kept running as the tree changes.** The team demos are the programs in `ProjectFortress/demos/`; no suite or step of the gate runs them. If a change breaks a demo and the way to repair the demo is known, the batch that makes the change also rewrites the demo. A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. For example, the change that made `10^(-4)` an error (P-153, the integer power) also wrote `10.0^(-4)` in `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, and `10.0^(-6)` for `10^(-6)` in `npbft.fss`. A demo that fails for want of a feature is made to run again once the feature is built. So the demos known to fail today are to be respelled where the way is known. Under walk, the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reach their end (F-283). The compiled checker refuses `trips.fss` (row 817), and the reductions that leave out the static argument of a big operator whose bound names its own static parameter, such as `SUM`; their repair writes the argument (row 731).
+- P-166 **`ZZ`'s and `QQ`'s values are value objects, and the specification's list of reference objects stops naming arbitrary-precision numbers.** The library declares `value object BigNum extends ZZ` (`LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:544`, `.fsi:196`), so every `ZZ` value is a value object, and `QQ`'s object `Ratio` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:648`) is a `value object` too. By the specification's rule two value objects of one type are strictly equivalent when their fields are, so two `ZZ` values built apart are `SEQV` when their integers are equal, `SEQV` converting each into its bits and comparing those, and two equal rationals built apart are `SEQV` in the same way. The specification's list in `Specification/basic/objects.tex` ("Reference objects include arbitrary-precision numbers") is revised to name them among the value objects, in the revision form (P-96) with one Appendix I entry. Why: the library's `value` declaration is the deliberate word, and where it is, the curator's rule brings the specification's example in line with the code. Detail: `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 2.4, point 11, which found the split.
+- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174); `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` where it is a size (P-40), and a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's four numbers (P-174). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. `gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). The parameter types of the declaration that a call runs are places that fix a type, and a numeral argument goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, by its own conversion if need be, with its default as the last resort: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, the numeral an `NN32` at `NN32`'s own `=` (P-46 gives the rule and its ground; rows 973 and 966 hold where walk departs). Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in two places, the numeral types, whose names and static parameters are the Draft's (P-174), and the places that fix no type, where the compiler's prelude, the team's later word, keeps the numeral's own type; the curator takes the bend by his right to finish the specification. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. The Draft's text that it contradicts, for Appendix I: numerals "not directly converted" and "polymorphic" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-141`) at places that fix no type, and a `nat` parameter usable wherever an `NN32` variable is (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:84-86`); P-174 names the binary chapter's, which it leaves out. What it keeps and changes in form: the judgement's section 3, but for the numeral types' form, which P-174 holds. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1 to 6 and the 42 test programs of its appendix; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`.

At a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter, a declared return type and a coercion it converts through the place type's coercion from `NaturalNumeral` or `RadixPointNumeral`, run with the four numbers bound as values of type `ZZ`, one result per site and type; a folded constant at a library number type converts from its exact value, outside the coercion; a numeral out of the type's range, one that rounds to an infinity at `RR32` or `RR64`, one at a type with no coercion from it, or one outside its coercion's `where` clause is refused there when it runs; a store keeps its default alone. - F-356 **In the fork/join shape that the library and the compiled runtime give parallel work, a Java model of microGPT's step with unboxed arrays runs 19 to 80 times slower than plain loops at the library's grains, and 1.4 to 4.8 times slower with the matrix product stopped at blocks of 16.** The library's range stops its split at 16 elements (`grainSize`, `Library/RangeInternals.fss`; P-175), and its matrix product splits down to single elements (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3044-3102`). The model is the baseline of F-355 with its vocabulary on a `ForkJoinPool` and plain loops at the leaves, so its times are a floor for compiled Fortress with this structure. At the library's grains a step takes 19 to 32 times the plain step on one thread, 55 times on two and 80 on four. Threads gain only from a product of about 128 by 128 with blocks of 64, and a dot product only from about 260,000 elements with a grain of 1,024; the model's products are 16 by 16 to 64 by 16. So at microGPT's sizes the library's parallel shape costs time at any thread count, and the matrix product's missing grain is the largest part of the cost. +- F-364 **The compiled checker instantiates a reduction that writes no static argument by its expected type, else by the type of its body, where the call as written is not accepted; a reduction that is accepted as written is unchanged.** For `__bigOperator(BIG OP(), clauses)` with no static argument written, `reductionApplication` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala`) first checks the call as written, where the big operator has an instance alone; if that is not accepted or its type does not convert to the expected type, it writes the static argument as the expected type, then as the body's type, each only where the type meets the bounds of the big operator's one static parameter, and takes the first form that is accepted and converts. +- F-366 **A numeral at a call goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, on both paths: a declaration that only the numeral's own coercion reaches runs in place of the one that fits the numeral at its default where its declared parameter types lie strictly below, by subtyping; otherwise the one that the default fits runs.** It builds P-46. So `u = 0` and `0 = u` are `true`, and `u =/= 0` is `false`, for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32`; `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`; `k(5)` runs `k(x: NN32)` beside `k(x: Any)`; a `case` clause `0` matches a zero `NN32`; and a program's own number type with a numeral coercion compares with a numeral by its own `=`. `Equality[\T\]` declares `opr =/=(self, other:T)` as the negation of the type's `=` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:102`), which a type that extends `Equality` reaches before the `=/=` over `Any` (`:98`). The order between the two kinds of declaration is subtyping on the declared parameter types, not the coercion chapter's relation: `f(1.5)` beside `f(x: RR32)` and `f(x: RR64)` runs the `RR64` declaration, and `x^2` for an `RR64` keeps its integer power. A value's coercion is not ranked so. Of two declarations reached only by coercion and not ordered, the one that the numeral's default fits runs, whether they differ at the numeral alone or elsewhere too, so `1.0 s` for `s: ZZ32` checks against the one library at `RR64`'s juxtaposition. So a model line may compare a number of any type with a numeral, and write a float numeral beside an integer value, on both paths. The checker does the comparison only where the declaration that fits has a numeral at a parameter that is not of the numeral's default type, so a call such as `i + 1` costs nothing more; walk keeps each choice in its dispatch cache, except one that asked a type of a program's own for its numeral coercion, whose `where` clause the cache's key does not hold. The key tells a negative constant from a numeral of the same default, since no unsigned type takes the first (`Numerals.rangeKey`). Two departures: under walk a numeral beside a value typed `Any` is converted by the value's run-time type (row 1016), and on both paths a numeral at a bare type parameter's declaration does not go to a more specific one (row 1017). Source: `numeralAttempt` and `numeralTie` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:980-1021`, `:1066`, `:1117`; `bestMatchForNumerals` and `belowByNumerals` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:2325-2428`. A parameter, of a function or a constructor, a local variable declared with an arrow type, and a variable of arrow type at an assignment, a mutable top-level variable among them, receive the instance that a direct call with arguments of the arrow's domain types runs (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Fcn.java`, `received`; `interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `instanceReceivedAt`). An overloaded name keeps its whole overload set, and its type as a value holds its generic overloads, so `pick(twice)` now runs an arrow-typed `pick` where it ran `pick(x: Any)` (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:2970`). Not built: an immutable top-level variable keeps the generic value (row 1019), and a callee's type parameter fixed only by a value's run-time type refuses the function (row 1018). +- F-368 **Under walk a top-level array literal with a declared type is built into the library array of that type, in the variable's cell.** `LazilyEvaluatedCell.getValueNull` builds an immutable variable's literal when the cell is first forced, so a reader above the declaration, an importer and `forVarDecl4`'s type check all see the array; `BuildEnvironments.forVarDecl4` builds a `var` variable's. +- F-369 **A top-level tuple binding compiles: each name is a top-level variable of its element's type, and the right side is evaluated once, at the first read of any name.** The checker gives the tuple that it rebuilds from the checked elements their tuple type, from which each name's thunk reads its own (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Decls.scala:272-277`); where only some names declare a type and the right side is no tuple expression of as many elements, it checks the right side again against each name's type (`Decls.scala:324-336`). So a model line of this form compiles as written, the model's lines 17 to 19 among them, and a name bound so is typed as a single binding's is: `explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss:77`, `beta1 m`, is a checker site against the one library that row 474 hid. +- P-46 **A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits, except a numeral's own conversion.** The declaration that runs is chosen on the parameter types that each overload declares: first those that apply, then the most specific of them (P-45). A generic declaration applies if some type within its bounds takes the arguments. Only then is the chosen declaration instantiated by promotion: at the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce (P-74). So beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` applies to a call with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, at `T = Number`. It is the more specific, so it runs, at `ZZ64`. Why: the curator wants fast generic code that a JVM can specialise. The exception is a numeral at a call. A comparison of a number with a numeral answers by the number's value, and the programmer does not retype the numeral: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, and no way that answers `false` is accepted. Of the ways to `true` that the review of them offers, the curator took its way B, whose rule is in the review's words, not his: a numeral is applicable to a parameter that fixes no type, at its default, and to a parameter whose type declares a coercion from the numeral's type, by that coercion (P-173); among the applicable declarations the most specific runs, and where two are not ordered, the one that the default fits. So `NN32`'s own `=` runs, and not the library's `=` over `(Any, Any)`, which the numeral fits at its default `ZZ32` and which answers `false` by `SEQV` (P-168). A value typed `Any` or `Number` fixes no type for the numeral beside it, which keeps its default. His own broader rule, to apply any conversion that reaches a specific declaration and to fall back to a plain one only when none does, so holds for a numeral's own conversion; for a value's coercion it is not taken. Walk and the compiled checker both infer static arguments with coercion, by the same promotion. The compiled path inserts the conversions statically. P-49 gives the order in which the checker tries a call. Row 537: the compiled dispatch between two generic declarations of one name with different bounds. Rows 973 and 966: walk answers `false` for `u = 0`, and `true` for `u =/= 0`, which follows `=`. Detail: `reviews/numeral-equality-ways-2026-11-10.md`, "Way B. A numeral goes to the most specific declaration that takes it; the default is the last resort".
+- P-78 **`SUM` and `PROD` are one generic reduction each over the library's algebra, in place of the team's catch-all over `Number`, and take their identity from the static argument.** `SUM` is generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `PROD` over `MultiplicativeRing`. A reduction written with generators writes its static argument where nothing at the call fixes the element type. The compiled checker fixes it from neither the generators, the body nor a declared type that receives the value, and refuses every such `SUM` or `PROD` that leaves it out (row 731, a gap of the checker). Row 731's workaround is to write it in every clause form of `SUM` and `PROD`, as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. A sum without generators is written as before, with no static argument: `SUM e` over a collection `e`, and the dot product `x DOT y`. `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN`, the team's `Number`-typed big operators for the maximum, the minimum and both, each with an identity, are gone; no program called them. `MAX` and `MIN` get no identity on the integers or the floats, so an empty `BIG MAX` or `BIG MIN` raises `EmptyReduction` (F-60: a maximum's identity is its type's least value, which a coercion into a wider type does not carry). Under walk, an empty `SUM` or `PROD` over another algebra, such as a user `AdditiveGroup`, still fails (row 436) until the specification's `HasIdentity` is built.
+- P-79 **Every team demo is kept running as the tree changes.** The team demos are the programs in `ProjectFortress/demos/`; no suite or step of the gate runs them. If a change breaks a demo and the way to repair the demo is known, the batch that makes the change also rewrites the demo. A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. For example, the change that made `10^(-4)` an error (P-153, the integer power) also wrote `10.0^(-4)` in `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, and `10.0^(-6)` for `10^(-6)` in `npbft.fss`. A demo that fails for want of a feature is made to run again once the feature is built. So the demos known to fail today are to be respelled where the way is known. Under walk, the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reach their end (F-283). The compiled checker refuses `trips.fss` (row 817), and the reductions that leave out the static argument of a big operator whose bound names its own static parameter, such as `SUM`; their repair writes the argument (row 731).
+- P-166 **`ZZ`'s and `QQ`'s values are value objects, and the specification's list of reference objects stops naming arbitrary-precision numbers.** The library declares `value object BigNum extends ZZ` (`LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:544`, `.fsi:196`), so every `ZZ` value is a value object, and `QQ`'s object `Ratio` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:648`) is a `value object` too. By the specification's rule two value objects of one type are strictly equivalent when their fields are, so two `ZZ` values built apart are `SEQV` when their integers are equal, `SEQV` converting each into its bits and comparing those, and two equal rationals built apart are `SEQV` in the same way. The specification's list in `Specification/basic/objects.tex` ("Reference objects include arbitrary-precision numbers") is revised to name them among the value objects, in the revision form (P-96) with one Appendix I entry. Why: the library's `value` declaration is the deliberate word, and where it is, the curator's rule brings the specification's example in line with the code. Detail: `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 2.4, point 11, which found the split.
+- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174); `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` where it is a size (P-40), and a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's four numbers (P-174). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. `gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). The parameter types of the declaration that a call runs are places that fix a type, and a numeral argument goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, by its own conversion if need be, with its default as the last resort: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, the numeral an `NN32` at `NN32`'s own `=` (P-46 gives the rule and its ground; rows 973 and 966 hold where walk departs). Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in two places, the numeral types, whose names and static parameters are the Draft's (P-174), and the places that fix no type, where the compiler's prelude, the team's later word, keeps the numeral's own type; the curator takes the bend by his right to finish the specification. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. The Draft's text that it contradicts, for Appendix I: numerals "not directly converted" and "polymorphic" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-141`) at places that fix no type, and a `nat` parameter usable wherever an `NN32` variable is (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:84-86`); P-174 names the binary chapter's, which it leaves out. What it keeps and changes in form: the judgement's section 3, but for the numeral types' form, which P-174 holds. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1 to 6 and the 42 test programs of its appendix; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`.

+- F-368 **Under walk a top-level array literal with a declared type is built into the library array of that type, in the variable's cell.** `LazilyEvaluatedCell.getValueNull` builds an immutable variable's literal when the cell is first forced, so a reader above the declaration, an importer and `forVarDecl4`'s type check all see the array; `BuildEnvironments.forVarDecl4` builds a `var` variable's. Both call `LHSEvaluator.topLevelArray`, which runs the block's code, `libraryArray`. So a table of the model can be a top-level literal with a declared type, as `shp: ZZ32[9] = [...]`, under walk; the compiled path is not touched. The declared size is checked only at the top level, by `forVarDecl4`; a block binds a literal of another size (row 1022). A field declaration of an object takes the same code. An untyped top-level literal stays a paste (row 49); a `var` bound in a block to a literal is immutable (row 1024), and a literal assigned to a variable is not built (row 1025). Tests: `tests/ObjectFieldArrayLiteral.fss`, `tests/TopLevelArrayLiteral.fss`, `TopLevelArrayLiteralSize.fss`, `TopLevelArrayLiteralElement.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-toplevel-array-literal/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".
+- F-369 **A top-level tuple binding compiles: each name is a top-level variable of its element's type, and the right side is evaluated once, at the first read of any name.** The checker gives the tuple that it rebuilds from the checked elements their tuple type, from which each name's thunk reads its own (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Decls.scala:272-277`); where only some names declare a type and the right side is no tuple expression of as many elements, it checks the right side again against each name's type (`Decls.scala:324-336`). The code generator keeps the right side's value in a hidden class `<Component>$tuple$<first name>` and gives each name its own class, whose initializer takes its element out by the tuple's typed getter (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:6528`); a wildcard binds nothing, and a binding of wildcards alone never evaluates its right side (row 1011). So a model line of this form compiles as written, the model's lines 17 to 19 among them, and a name bound so is typed as a single binding's is: `explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss:77`, `beta1 m`, is a checker site against the one library that row 474 hid. Under walk the same right side runs once for each name and once more (row 1026). A local tuple binding's declared name beside untyped names is still unchecked (row 1029). Tests: `compiler_tests/TopLevelTupleBindingCompiled.test`, `TopLevelTupleBindingImport.test`, `TopLevelTupleBindingMixedTypes.test`, `XXXTopLevelTupleBindingType.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-tuple-binding/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "The binding as compiled".
+- P-46 **A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits, except a numeral's own conversion.** The declaration that runs is chosen on the parameter types that each overload declares: first those that apply, then the most specific of them (P-45). A generic declaration applies if some type within its bounds takes the arguments. Only then is the chosen declaration instantiated by promotion: at the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce (P-74). So beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` applies to a call with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, at `T = Number`. It is the more specific, so it runs, at `ZZ64`. Why: the curator wants fast generic code that a JVM can specialise. The exception is a numeral at a call. A comparison of a number with a numeral answers by the number's value, and the programmer does not retype the numeral: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, and no way that answers `false` is accepted. Of the ways to `true` that the review of them offers, the curator took its way B, whose rule is in the review's words, not his: a numeral is applicable to a parameter that fixes no type, at its default, and to a parameter whose type declares a coercion from the numeral's type, by that coercion (P-173); among the applicable declarations the most specific runs, and where two are not ordered, the one that the default fits. So `NN32`'s own `=` runs, and not the library's `=` over `(Any, Any)`, which the numeral fits at its default `ZZ32` and which answers `false` by `SEQV` (P-168). A value typed `Any` or `Number` fixes no type for the numeral beside it, which keeps its default. His own broader rule, to apply any conversion that reaches a specific declaration and to fall back to a plain one only when none does, so holds for a numeral's own conversion; for a value's coercion it is not taken. Walk and the compiled checker both infer static arguments with coercion, by the same promotion. The compiled path inserts the conversions statically. P-49 gives the order in which the checker tries a call. Row 537: the compiled dispatch between two generic declarations of one name with different bounds. Rows 973 and 966: walk answers `false` for `u = 0`, and `true` for `u =/= 0`, which follows `=`. Detail: `reviews/numeral-equality-ways-2026-11-10.md`, "Way B. A numeral goes to the most specific declaration that takes it; the default is the last resort".
+- P-78 **`SUM` and `PROD` are one generic reduction each over the library's algebra, in place of the team's catch-all over `Number`, and take their identity from the static argument.** `SUM` is generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `PROD` over `MultiplicativeRing`. A reduction written with generators writes its static argument where nothing at the call fixes the element type. The compiled checker fixes it from neither the generators, the body nor a declared type that receives the value, and refuses every such `SUM` or `PROD` that leaves it out (row 731, a gap of the checker). Row 731's workaround is to write it in every clause form of `SUM` and `PROD`, as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. A sum without generators is written as before, with no static argument: `SUM e` over a collection `e`, and the dot product `x DOT y`. `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN`, the team's `Number`-typed big operators for the maximum, the minimum and both, each with an identity, are gone; no program called them. `MAX` and `MIN` get no identity on the integers or the floats, so an empty `BIG MAX` or `BIG MIN` raises `EmptyReduction` (F-60: a maximum's identity is its type's least value, which a coercion into a wider type does not carry). Under walk, an empty `SUM` or `PROD` over another algebra, such as a user `AdditiveGroup`, still fails (row 436) until the specification's `HasIdentity` is built.
+- P-79 **Every team demo is kept running as the tree changes.** The team demos are the programs in `ProjectFortress/demos/`; no suite or step of the gate runs them. If a change breaks a demo and the way to repair the demo is known, the batch that makes the change also rewrites the demo. A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. For example, the change that made `10^(-4)` an error (P-153, the integer power) also wrote `10.0^(-4)` in `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, and `10.0^(-6)` for `10^(-6)` in `npbft.fss`. A demo that fails for want of a feature is made to run again once the feature is built. So the demos known to fail today are to be respelled where the way is known. Under walk, the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reach their end (F-283). The compiled checker refuses `trips.fss` (row 817), and the reductions that leave out the static argument of a big operator whose bound names its own static parameter, such as `SUM`; their repair writes the argument (row 731).
+- P-166 **`ZZ`'s and `QQ`'s values are value objects, and the specification's list of reference objects stops naming arbitrary-precision numbers.** The library declares `value object BigNum extends ZZ` (`LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:544`, `.fsi:196`), so every `ZZ` value is a value object, and `QQ`'s object `Ratio` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:648`) is a `value object` too. By the specification's rule two value objects of one type are strictly equivalent when their fields are, so two `ZZ` values built apart are `SEQV` when their integers are equal, `SEQV` converting each into its bits and comparing those, and two equal rationals built apart are `SEQV` in the same way. The specification's list in `Specification/basic/objects.tex` ("Reference objects include arbitrary-precision numbers") is revised to name them among the value objects, in the revision form (P-96) with one Appendix I entry. Why: the library's `value` declaration is the deliberate word, and where it is, the curator's rule brings the specification's example in line with the code. Detail: `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 2.4, point 11, which found the split.
+- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174); `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` where it is a size (P-40), and a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's four numbers (P-174). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. `gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). The parameter types of the declaration that a call runs are places that fix a type, and a numeral argument goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, by its own conversion if need be, with its default as the last resort: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, the numeral an `NN32` at `NN32`'s own `=` (P-46 gives the rule and its ground; rows 973 and 966 hold where walk departs). Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in two places, the numeral types, whose names and static parameters are the Draft's (P-174), and the places that fix no type, where the compiler's prelude, the team's later word, keeps the numeral's own type; the curator takes the bend by his right to finish the specification. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. The Draft's text that it contradicts, for Appendix I: numerals "not directly converted" and "polymorphic" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-141`) at places that fix no type, and a `nat` parameter usable wherever an `NN32` variable is (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:84-86`); P-174 names the binary chapter's, which it leaves out. What it keeps and changes in form: the judgement's section 3, but for the numeral types' form, which P-174 holds. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1 to 6 and the 42 test programs of its appendix; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`.

lines: - F-356 **In the fork/join shape that the library and the compiled runtime give parallel work, a Java model of microGPT's step with unboxed arrays runs 19 to 80 times slower than plain loops at the library's grains, and 1.4 to 4.8 times slower with the matrix product stopped at blocks of 16.** The library's range stops its split at 16 elements (`grainSize`, `Library/RangeInternals.fss`; P-175), and its matrix product splits down to single elements (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3044-3102`). The model is the baseline of F-355 with its vocabulary on a `ForkJoinPool` and plain loops at the leaves, so its times are a floor for compiled Fortress with this structure. At the library's grains a step takes 19 to 32 times the plain step on one thread, 55 times on two and 80 on four. Threads gain only from a product of about 128 by 128 with blocks of 64, and a dot product only from about 260,000 elements with a grain of 1,024; the model's products are 16 by 16 to 64 by 16. So at microGPT's sizes the library's parallel shape costs time at any thread count, and the matrix product's missing grain is the largest part of the cost. Measured once on a shared machine of 4 CPUs; every configuration passes the checks. Commands: `java-baseline/run.sh steps`, `kernels` and `scale`. Detail: `java-baseline/REPORT.md`, "6. Fork/join: the baseline in the shape of the library and the compiled runtime".

- F-362 **The signs for sum and product are accumulators, and an api's operator header takes what a component's takes.** U+2211 and U+220F parse as `SUM` and `PROD` in a reduction and in an operator's declaration and are no `Op` anywhere, so a program's own `opr ∑` declares `BIG +`, and an infix or postfix use of either sign is a `Syntax Error`; so is `opr ∑` or `opr SUM` in an import's list, a gap whose way round is `except { opr BIG + }` (row 42); an api declares `opr (x: T)^T` and the other postfix exponent operators as a component does. A grammar edit regenerates the two tracked parsers, `parser/Fortress.java` and `parser/templateparser/TemplateParser.java`. So on both paths a model line can write `∑` for `SUM`, and the helper file's api can declare `^T`; no test applies the sign to an array. Tests: `tests/SumSignAccumulator.fss`, `tests/ApiPostfixExponentOp.fss`, `compiler_tests/SumSignAccumulatorCompiled.test`, `compiler_tests/ApiPostfixExponentOpCompiled.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-parser-declarations/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "Programs run old against new".

- F-363 **A superscript follows a dotted access and a parenthesised call on both paths.** `p.wq^T`, `B.n^2`, `B.f()^T` and `B.data[5]^2` parse as the operator applied to the whole dotted primary to its left, and `(f(x))^T`, `(f(x))!` and `(a^b)!` run under walk as they do compiled; `f(x)^T` and `f(x)^2` stay a static error on both paths (walk: "the argument should not be immediately followed by a non-expression element"; the checker: "Item at this location must be an expression, not an operator."). The parser reads a primary with a dot as the front of the math items that follow it (`parser/Expression.rats:386-400`), so a subscript, a parenthesised item or a tight identifier after a dotted method call parses too, which no test asserts; the one node kind it builds for a single item is the one the parenthesised spelling built, so neither the checker nor the code generator changed. Walk's postfix branch evaluates an operand in parentheses as one expression (`interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:965-970`). So a model line may write `p.wq^T x` and `(onehot(ks, 5))^T dx`; a selector after a superscript, `B.data^T.v`, is still a syntax error, and a subscript math item followed by a superscript, `x[5]^2` or `B.f()[5]^2`, still fails on both paths (row 1 under walk, row 1005 compiled). Tests: `tests/SuperscriptAfterDottedAccess.fss`, `tests/SuperscriptAfterParenthesisedCall.fss`, `tests/SuperscriptAfterCallRefused.fss` with its `.test`, and `compiler_tests/SuperscriptAfterDottedAccessCompiled.test`, `SuperscriptAfterParenthesisedCallCompiled.test`, `XXXSuperscriptAfterCallRefusedCompiled.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-superscript-after/REPORT.md`, "Each form on the base and after" and "The trees".

-- F-364 **The compiled checker instantiates a reduction that writes no static argument by its expected type, else by the type of its body, where the call as written is not accepted; a reduction that is accepted as written is unchanged.** For `__bigOperator(BIG OP(), clauses)` with no static argument written, `reductionApplication` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala`) first checks the call as written, where the big operator has an instance alone; if that is not accepted or its type does not convert to the expected type, it writes the static argument as the expected type, then as the body's type, each only where the type meets the bounds of the big operator's one static parameter, and takes the first form that is accepted and converts. The elements are converted to the instance. A call's argument has no expected type where the call is accepted without one (P-51), so a reduction there runs at its body's type. So `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MIN` and `BIG MAX` need no written static argument for the checker; the library and the model still write it (F-285, F-59). The two paths give such a reduction different instances at a method's return type, a field, a top-level variable and an assignment (row 1008), so a program for both paths writes the argument there. A big operator with two or more static parameters is still refused (row 1007). The library's three sites unwritten give 3 errors on the base and 0 on the tree; `explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss:43` unwritten, 43 errors on the base and 42 on the tree, the one gone at `:43`. Tests: `compiler_tests/InferBigOperatorSelfBound`; guards `compiler_tests/InferBigOperatorExpectedType` and `InferBigOperatorUnwritten`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-static-argument-inferred/REPORT.md`, "Step 1, row 731: the reduction", "5. Old against new" and "7. The stages and the checker's time".

+- F-364 **The compiled checker instantiates a reduction that writes no static argument by its expected type, else by the type of its body, where the call as written is not accepted; a reduction that is accepted as written is unchanged.** For `__bigOperator(BIG OP(), clauses)` with no static argument written, `reductionApplication` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala`) first checks the call as written, where the big operator has an instance alone; if that is not accepted or its type does not convert to the expected type, it writes the static argument as the expected type, then as the body's type, each only where the type meets the bounds of the big operator's one static parameter, and takes the first form that is accepted and converts. The elements are converted to the instance. A call's argument has no expected type where the call is accepted without one (P-51), so a reduction there runs at its body's type. So `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MIN` and `BIG MAX` need no written static argument for the checker; the library and the model still write it (F-285, F-59). The two paths give such a reduction different instances at a method's return type, a field, a top-level variable and an assignment (row 1008), so a program for both paths writes the argument there. A big operator with two or more static parameters is still refused (row 1007), and where the bound names its parameter, a type error in an unwritten reduction's body is reported as the big operator's refusal (row 1015). Observed once, in copies with the argument removed: the library's two `BIG MIN` sites and its list comprehension (F-285), and `explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss:43`, give no error. Tests: `compiler_tests/InferBigOperatorSelfBound`; guards `compiler_tests/InferBigOperatorExpectedType` and `InferBigOperatorUnwritten`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-static-argument-inferred/REPORT.md`, "Step 1, row 731: the reduction", "5. Old against new" and "7. The stages and the checker's time".

- F-365 **The compiled checker instantiates a reference to a generic function by the arrow type that receives it, and refuses one that the arrow type leaves open.** A functional reference with one declaration that has static parameters, no written static arguments and an expected arrow type takes the static arguments that make its instance a subtype of that type (`instantiatedReference`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala`); as an argument it is typed again in the retry with each candidate's parameter type (`retypable`). A static parameter that the arrow type's domain does not fix, one that only the return type mentions among them, is refused: 'A reference to the generic function pick takes its static arguments from the arrow type that receives it, and ZZ32->ZZ32 does not fix B.' An arrow type that carries its own static parameters is a subtype of no arrow type and coerces to nothing (`scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala`, `scala_src/typechecker/CoercionOracle.scala:292-293`). The applied value of an untyped binding is refused with a message. A static parameter of the function's own counts as unbound also where the kind environment holds its name for another declaration's parameter, as inside a generic declaration that calls its static parameter the same (`carriesOwnStaticParams`, `TypeAnalyzer.scala`), and the memo of normalized arrow types keys an arrow type by its static parameters too, so that a generic function's type and an instance written alike are not taken for each other. So the compiled half of the model's row lift, `rows(rmsn, x)` with a sized `rmsn`, has its checker. Still refused or stopped: a name with several declarations of which one is generic (row 1009), an untyped binding never applied (row 1010). Still accepted, and then dead at run time: a reference whose expected type is not an arrow type, as at a parameter of type `Any` (row 1012). Tests: `compiler_tests/GenericFunctionAsValueCompiled`, `GenericFunctionAsValueSameNameCompiled`, `XXXGenericFunctionAsValueOpenCompiled`, `XXXGenericFunctionAsValueUntypedCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-static-argument-inferred/REPORT.md`, "Step 2, row 758: the reference to a generic function" and "5. Old against new".

- F-366 **A numeral at a call goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, on both paths: a declaration that only the numeral's own coercion reaches runs in place of the one that fits the numeral at its default where its declared parameter types lie strictly below, by subtyping; otherwise the one that the default fits runs.** It builds P-46. So `u = 0` and `0 = u` are `true`, and `u =/= 0` is `false`, for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32`; `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`; `k(5)` runs `k(x: NN32)` beside `k(x: Any)`; a `case` clause `0` matches a zero `NN32`; and a program's own number type with a numeral coercion compares with a numeral by its own `=`. `Equality[\T\]` declares `opr =/=(self, other:T)` as the negation of the type's `=` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:102`), which a type that extends `Equality` reaches before the `=/=` over `Any` (`:98`). The order between the two kinds of declaration is subtyping on the declared parameter types, not the coercion chapter's relation: `f(1.5)` beside `f(x: RR32)` and `f(x: RR64)` runs the `RR64` declaration, and `x^2` for an `RR64` keeps its integer power. A value's coercion is not ranked so. Of two declarations reached only by coercion and not ordered, the one that the numeral's default fits runs, whether they differ at the numeral alone or elsewhere too, so `1.0 s` for `s: ZZ32` checks against the one library at `RR64`'s juxtaposition. So a model line may compare a number of any type with a numeral, and write a float numeral beside an integer value, on both paths. The checker does the comparison only where the declaration that fits has a numeral at a parameter that is not of the numeral's default type, so a call such as `i + 1` costs nothing more; walk keeps each choice in its dispatch cache, except one that asked a type of a program's own for its numeral coercion, whose `where` clause the cache's key does not hold. The key tells a negative constant from a numeral of the same default, since no unsigned type takes the first (`Numerals.rangeKey`). Two departures: under walk a numeral beside a value typed `Any` is converted by the value's run-time type (row 1016), and on both paths a numeral at a bare type parameter's declaration does not go to a more specific one (row 1017). Source: `numeralAttempt` and `numeralTie` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:980-1021`, `:1066`, `:1117`; `bestMatchForNumerals` and `belowByNumerals` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:2325-2428`. Tests: `compiler_tests/NumeralMostSpecificCompiled`, `compiler_tests/NumeralTieDefaultCompiled`, `tests/NumeralMostSpecificWalk`, `tests/NumeralEqualsNumberWalk`, `tests/NotEqualNumeral`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-most-specific/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why" and "5. Points to report".

- F-367 **Under walk a generic function is a value, received at the arrow type of its parameter or variable.** A function with static parameters has a type of its own as a value (`interpreter/evaluator/types/FTypeGenericArrow.java`), below `Any` and below each arrow type it can be received at. A parameter, of a function or a constructor, a local variable declared with an arrow type, and a variable of arrow type at an assignment, a mutable top-level variable among them, receive the instance that a direct call with arguments of the arrow's domain types runs (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Fcn.java`, `received`; `interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `instanceReceivedAt`). A parameter, of a function or a constructor, a local variable declared with an arrow type, and a variable of arrow type at an assignment, a mutable top-level variable among them, receive the instance that a direct call with arguments of the arrow's domain types runs (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Fcn.java`, `received`; `interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `instanceReceivedAt`). +- P-46 **A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits, except a numeral's own conversion.** The declaration that runs is chosen on the parameter types that each overload declares: first those that apply, then the most specific of them (P-45). A generic declaration applies if some type within its bounds takes the arguments. Only then is the chosen declaration instantiated by promotion: at the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce (P-74). So beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` applies to a call with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, at `T = Number`. It is the more specific, so it runs, at `ZZ64`. Why: the curator wants fast generic code that a JVM can specialise. The exception is a numeral at a call. A comparison of a number with a numeral answers by the number's value, and the programmer does not retype the numeral: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, and no way that answers `false` is accepted. Of the ways to `true` that the review of them offers, the curator took its way B, whose rule is in the review's words, not his: a numeral is applicable to a parameter that fixes no type, at its default, and to a parameter whose type declares a coercion from the numeral's type, by that coercion (P-173); among the applicable declarations the most specific runs, and where two are not ordered, the one that the default fits. So `NN32`'s own `=` runs, and not the library's `=` over `(Any, Any)`, which the numeral fits at its default `ZZ32` and which answers `false` by `SEQV` (P-168). A value typed `Any` or `Number` fixes no type for the numeral beside it, which keeps its default. His own broader rule, to apply any conversion that reaches a specific declaration and to fall back to a plain one only when none does, so holds for a numeral's own conversion; for a value's coercion it is not taken. Walk and the compiled checker both infer static arguments with coercion, by the same promotion. The compiled path inserts the conversions statically. A numeral goes to the most specific declaration that takes it; the default is the last resort".

A reduction written with generators writes its static argument where nothing at the call fixes the element type. The compiled checker fixes it from neither the generators, the body nor a declared type that receives the value, and refuses every such `SUM` or `PROD` that leaves it out (row 731, a gap of the checker). +- P-79 **Every team demo is kept running as the tree changes.** The team demos are the programs in `ProjectFortress/demos/`; no suite or step of the gate runs them. If a change breaks a demo and the way to repair the demo is known, the batch that makes the change also rewrites the demo. A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. +- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174); `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` where it is a size (P-40), and a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's four numbers (P-174). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. `gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). The parameter types of the declaration that a call runs are places that fix a type, and a numeral argument goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, by its own conversion if need be, with its default as the last resort: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, the numeral an `NN32` at `NN32`'s own `=` (P-46 gives the rule and its ground; rows 973 and 966 hold where walk departs). Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in two places, the numeral types, whose names and static parameters are the Draft's (P-174), and the places that fix no type, where the compiler's prelude, the team's later word, keeps the numeral's own type; the curator takes the bend by his right to finish the specification. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. The Draft's text that it contradicts, for Appendix I: numerals "not directly converted" and "polymorphic" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-141`) at places that fix no type, and a `nat` parameter usable wherever an `NN32` variable is (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:84-86`); P-174 names the binary chapter's, which it leaves out. What it keeps and changes in form: the judgement's section 3, but for the numeral types' form, which P-174 holds. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1 to 6 and the 42 test programs of its appendix; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`.

A static parameter that the arrow type's domain does not fix, one that only the return type mentions among them, is refused: 'A reference to the generic function pick takes its static arguments from the arrow type that receives it, and ZZ32->ZZ32 does not fix B.' An arrow type that carries its own static parameters is a subtype of no arrow type and coerces to nothing (`scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala`, `scala_src/typechecker/CoercionOracle.scala:292-293`). The applied value of an untyped binding is refused with a message. A static parameter of the function's own counts as unbound also where the kind environment holds its name for another declaration's parameter, as inside a generic declaration that calls its static parameter the same (`carriesOwnStaticParams`, `TypeAnalyzer.scala`), and the memo of normalized arrow types keys an arrow type by its static parameters too, so that a generic function's type and an instance written alike are not taken for each other. The test passes a sized generic function to a callee that is not generic; no test compiles the form of the model's row lift, `rows(rmsn, x)`, a generic callee whose sizes its other argument fixes. +- F-366 **A numeral at a call goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, on both paths: a declaration that only the numeral's own coercion reaches runs in place of the one that fits the numeral at its default where its declared parameter types lie strictly below, by subtyping; otherwise the one that the default fits runs.** It builds P-46. The order between the two kinds of declaration is subtyping on the declared parameter types, not the coercion chapter's relation: `f(1.5)` beside `f(x: RR32)` and `f(x: RR64)` runs the `RR64` declaration, and `x^2` for an `RR64` keeps its integer power. A value's coercion is not ranked so. Of two declarations reached only by coercion and not ordered, the one that the numeral's default fits runs, whether they differ at the numeral alone or elsewhere too, so `1.0 s` for `s: ZZ32` checks against the one library at `RR64`'s juxtaposition. So a model line may compare a number of any type with a numeral, and write a float numeral beside an integer value, on both paths. The checker does the comparison only where the declaration that fits has a numeral at a parameter that is not of the numeral's default type, so a call such as `i + 1` costs nothing more; walk keeps each choice in its dispatch cache, except one that asked a type of a program's own for its numeral coercion, whose `where` clause the cache's key does not hold. The key tells a negative constant from a numeral of the same default, since no unsigned type takes the first (`Numerals.rangeKey`). Two departures: under walk a numeral beside a value typed `Any` is converted by the value's run-time type (row 1016), and on both paths a numeral at a bare type parameter's declaration does not go to a more specific one (row 1017). Source: `numeralAttempt` and `numeralTie` in `scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:980-1021`, `:1066`, `:1117`; `bestMatchForNumerals` and `belowByNumerals` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:2325-2428`. Tests: `compiler_tests/NumeralMostSpecificCompiled`, `compiler_tests/NumeralTieDefaultCompiled`, `tests/NumeralMostSpecificWalk`, `tests/NumeralEqualsNumberWalk`, `tests/NotEqualNumeral`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-most-specific/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why" and "5. Points to report".
+- F-367 **Under walk a generic function is a value, received at the arrow type of its parameter or variable.** A function with static parameters has a type of its own as a value (`interpreter/evaluator/types/FTypeGenericArrow.java`), below `Any` and below each arrow type it can be received at. A parameter, of a function or a constructor, a local variable declared with an arrow type, and a variable of arrow type at an assignment, a mutable top-level variable among them, receive the instance that a direct call with arguments of the arrow's domain types runs (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Fcn.java`, `received`; `interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `instanceReceivedAt`). A generic callee's static parameters are fixed by its other arguments first, so the row lift `rows(rmsn, x)` runs with a sized `rmsn`. Where the arrow type leaves a static parameter of the function open, and at `Any`, a type parameter or an untyped place, the value stays generic and each application infers its static arguments, as a direct call does; the compiled checker refuses those forms (row 1021). An overloaded name keeps its whole overload set, and its type as a value holds its generic overloads, so `pick(twice)` now runs an arrow-typed `pick` where it ran `pick(x: Any)` (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:2970`). Not built: an immutable top-level variable keeps the generic value (row 1019), and a callee's type parameter fixed only by a value's run-time type refuses the function (row 1018). A function declared in a block with static parameters of its own does not run under walk at all, called or passed (row 1020). Tests: `tests/GenericFunctionAsValueWalk.fss`, `GenericFunctionRowLiftWalk.fss`, `GenericFunctionAssignedWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-function-value/REPORT.md`, "The rule as built" and "Runs to report, not tests".
+- F-368 **Under walk a top-level array literal with a declared type is built into the library array of that type, in the variable's cell.** `LazilyEvaluatedCell.getValueNull` builds an immutable variable's literal when the cell is first forced, so a reader above the declaration, an importer and `forVarDecl4`'s type check all see the array; `BuildEnvironments.forVarDecl4` builds a `var` variable's. Both call `LHSEvaluator.topLevelArray`, which runs the block's code, `libraryArray`. So a table of the model can be a top-level literal with a declared type, as `shp: ZZ32[9] = [...]`, under walk; the compiled path is not touched. The declared size is checked only at the top level, by `forVarDecl4`; a block binds a literal of another size (row 1022). A field declaration of an object takes the same code. An untyped top-level literal stays a paste (row 49); a `var` bound in a block to a literal is immutable (row 1024), and a literal assigned to a variable is not built (row 1025). +- F-369 **A top-level tuple binding compiles: each name is a top-level variable of its element's type, and the right side is evaluated once, at the first read of any name.** The checker gives the tuple that it rebuilds from the checked elements their tuple type, from which each name's thunk reads its own (`scala_src/typechecker/impls/Decls.scala:272-277`); where only some names declare a type and the right side is no tuple expression of as many elements, it checks the right side again against each name's type (`Decls.scala:324-336`). The code generator keeps the right side's value in a hidden class `<Component>$tuple$<first name>` and gives each name its own class, whose initializer takes its element out by the tuple's typed getter (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:6528`); a wildcard binds nothing, and a binding of wildcards alone never evaluates its right side (row 1011). So a model line of this form compiles as written, the model's lines 17 to 19 among them, and a name bound so is typed as a single binding's is: `explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss:77`, `beta1 m`, is a checker site against the one library that row 474 hid.
